blocks.content: This topic goes past the Architecture module's overview into the two real implementation modes kube-proxy can run in, and the actual performance difference between them at real cluster scale.

As covered in the Architecture module, kube-proxy implements the actual networking rules that route a Service's virtual IP to real, current backing Pods, this topic covers precisely how, at the implementation level.

blocks.alt: The role already covered, this topic goes into precisely how it is implemented

blocks.content: In iptables mode, the historical default, kube-proxy programs a sequence of Linux iptables rules, a packet is checked against these rules roughly in order, meaning lookup cost grows with the total number of rules, and therefore, roughly, the number of Services.

blocks.alt: Rules checked roughly in sequence, cost growing with the total rule count

blocks.content: The IPVS mode uses the Linux kernel's IP Virtual Server subsystem instead, backed by a hash table rather than a sequential rule list, giving it a fundamentally more efficient, closer to constant-time, lookup regardless of how many Services exist.

blocks.alt: A hash-table lookup, fundamentally different, and more efficient, than a sequential scan

blocks.content: 4. Why This Matters at Real Scale
blocks.text: 4. Why This Matters at Real Scale

blocks.content: In a cluster with a genuinely large number of Services, iptables mode's lookup performance measurably degrades, IPVS mode stays meaningfully flatter, this is exactly why very large production clusters commonly choose IPVS mode deliberately.

blocks.alt: A real, measurable difference, worth knowing about at genuine production scale

blocks.content: This is not a fixed, unchangeable setting, kube-proxy's mode is configurable per cluster, letting operators choose based on their actual scale and needs, rather than being locked into whichever mode happened to be the historical default.

blocks.alt: A deliberate, configurable choice, not a permanent, fixed default

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kube-proxy can run in iptables mode (sequential rule chains) or IPVS mode (hash-table based lookup), a genuine implementation-level difference, not just a naming choice.
IPVS scales more gracefully as the number of Services grows, which is exactly why very large production clusters commonly choose it deliberately over the historical iptables default.
